subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Antimatter Asymmetry
description: Learn Antimatter Asymmetry in one minute.

hook.text: The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter. They'd annihilate, leaving nothing. Yet here we are.

buildup.text: For every billion antimatter particles, the Big Bang made one billion and one matter particles. That tiny excess is all we see.

discovery.text: CP violation—where matter and antimatter behave slightly differently—was found in 1964. But it's not enough to explain the gap.

twist.text: The full explanation is unknown. New physics beyond the Standard Model is needed to account for our existence.

climax.text: Experiments at CERN and neutrino detectors worldwide are searching for the missing piece. The answer may rewrite particle physics.

punchline.text: One extra particle per billion. That tiny imbalance built every star, planet, and person.

quiz.question: What is the antimatter asymmetry problem?
options: The Big Bang should have made equal matter and antimatter, yet the universe is almost entirely matter
Antimatter is more abundant than matter but can't be detected by telescopes
Dark matter is actually antimatter that has been hiding in the cosmic void

details.summary: The Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other completely — leaving a universe of pure energy. Instead, a tiny excess of matter survived, forming everything we see.
details.whyItMatters: Without this asymmetry, neither galaxies, stars, nor life could exist. Understanding why matter won over antimatter would solve one of the most fundamental questions about why the universe exists as it does.
takeaways: The Big Bang should have created equal matter and antimatter
A tiny matter excess survived mutual annihilation
Explaining this asymmetry remains an unsolved puzzle

faq.question: What is antimatter exactly?
faq.answer: Antimatter consists of particles with the same mass but opposite charge and quantum numbers as normal matter. A positron is the antimatter counterpart of an electron; an antiproton mirrors a proton. When matter meets antimatter, both annihilate into pure energy.

faq.question: What theories explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry?
faq.answer: The Sakharov conditions (1967) require baryon number violation, CP violation (matter/antimatter behaving differently), and departure from thermal equilibrium. The Standard Model contains some CP violation but not nearly enough.
